title: Growth Modeling with fit_bayesian_growth()
text: fit_bayesian_growth() function fits von Bertalanffy, Gompertz, Logistic growth models using Bayesian methods. key innovation maturity-based parameterization, derives growth coefficient \(k\) observable maturity metrics rather estimating directly.

title: Growth Modeling with fit_bayesian_growth()
text: von Bertalanffy (model = "v"): \[L(t) = L_\infty - (L_\infty - L_0) e^{-kt}\] Gompertz (model = "g"): \[L(t) = L_\infty \exp\left[-\ln\left(\frac{L_\infty}{L_0}\right) e^{-kt}\right]\] Logistic (model = "l"): \[L(t) = \frac{L_\infty}{1 + \left(\frac{L_\infty}{L_0} - 1\right) e^{-kt}}\]

title: Growth Modeling with fit_bayesian_growth()
text: Directly estimates growth coefficient \(k\):
code: library(vitalBayes) library(data.table)  # Load simulated data data(growth_data)  # Filter to non-embryos with age data gdata <- growth_data[embryo == FALSE & !is.na(age)]  # Traditional k-based von Bertalanffy growth_k <- fit_bayesian_growth(   lt      = "fl",   age     = "age",   sex     = "sex",   data    = gdata,   model   = "v",   k_based = TRUE,   CV_k    = 0.5,        # 50% CV on k prior (high uncertainty)   parallel = TRUE )  growth_k$summary(c("Linf", "L0", "k", "sigma"))

title: Growth Modeling with fit_bayesian_growth()
text: Derives \(k\) maturity parameters (\(L_{mat}\), \(t_{mat}\)), ensuring biological consistency: \[k = \frac{1}{t_{mat}} \ln\left(\frac{L_\infty - L_0}{L_\infty - L_{mat}}\right)\] maturity-based? Reduced correlation: \((L_\infty, k)\) notoriously correlated; maturity parameters break Observable anchoring: Maturity milestones fall within data range, unlike \(L_\infty\) Prior propagation: Uncertainty maturity models flows growth estimates Biological coherence: growth curve must pass \((t_{mat}, L_{mat})\) full derivation, see Maturity-Based Parameterization section Statistical Methods guide.
code: # First, fit maturity models mat_data <- growth_data[embryo == FALSE & !is.na(mat)]  L50_fit <- fit_bayesian_maturity(   maturity = "mat", lt = "fl", sex = "sex",   data = mat_data,   use_pooling = TRUE )  t50_fit <- fit_bayesian_maturity(   maturity = "mat", age = "age", sex = "sex",   data = mat_data[!is.na(age)],   use_pooling = TRUE )  # Optional: fit birth model for L0 prior birth_fit <- fit_bayesian_birth(   embryo_lts = growth_data[embryo == TRUE, fl],   free_swimming_lts = growth_data[embryo == FALSE, fl] )  # Maturity-based growth model growth_mat <- fit_bayesian_growth(   lt        = "fl",   age       = "age",   sex       = "sex",   data      = gdata,   model     = "v",   k_based   = FALSE,                    # Use maturity-based parameterization   length.mature_stanfit = L50_fit,      # Provides Lmat prior   age.mature_stanfit    = t50_fit,      # Provides tmat prior   birth_stanfit         = birth_fit,    # Provides L0 prior   parallel  = TRUE )  # k is now a derived quantity growth_mat$summary(c("Linf", "L0", "Lmat", "tmat", "k", "sigma"))

title: Natural Mortality Estimation with get_stochastic_mortality()
text: Natural mortality (\(M\)) — death causes fishing — among difficult parameters estimate fisheries biology. Direct observation rarely possible, rely indirect methods derive mortality life history parameters. approaches introduce uncertainty must properly propagated downstream analyses. get_stochastic_mortality() function implements Monte Carlo simulation age-specific mortality schedules full uncertainty propagation growth model posteriors. key innovation growth-model-agnostic estimation: mortality can derived von Bertalanffy, Gompertz, Logistic growth fits without theoretical compromise. vignette covers three available mortality models, growth-model-agnostic architecture, scaling approaches, integration broader vitalBayes workflow.

title: Natural Mortality Estimation with get_stochastic_mortality()
text: Chen-Watanabe model assumes natural mortality inversely related body size von Bertalanffy growth dynamics. vitalBayes implements L₀-parameterized version eliminates dependence theoretical parameter \(t_0\): \[M(t) = \frac{k \cdot L_\infty}{L(t)}\] \(L(t) = L_\infty - (L_\infty - L_0)e^{-kt}\) predicted length age \(t\). reformulation uses observable quantities (\(L_0\), birth length) rather mathematical abstractions (\(t_0\), age length zero). See vignette("chen_watanabe_reparameterization") full mathematical derivation. Two-phase extension. original CW model produces mortality declines asymptotically \(k\), biologically unrealistic — mortality increase old ages due senescence. two-phase extension models late-life mortality increase via Gompertz logistic functions, producing realistic bathtub-shaped mortality curves. use CW. Species juvenile mortality high declines size; species documented senescence patterns; situations theoretical grounding CW (von Bertalanffy derivation) appropriate.

title: Natural Mortality Estimation with get_stochastic_mortality()
text: Peterson-Wroblewski model takes purely allometric approach: \[M(W) = 1.92 \cdot W^{-0.25}\] \(W\) body weight grams. captures well-documented pattern smaller individuals experience higher mortality, -0.25 exponent reflecting metabolic scaling. Requirements. length-weight function needed convert predicted lengths body mass. use PW. Species well-characterized length-weight relationships; comparative studies across taxa; situations want simple, empirically-grounded model without growth model assumptions.

title: Natural Mortality Estimation with get_stochastic_mortality()
text: Lorenzen offers two formulations: Weight-based (1996): \[M(W) = \alpha \cdot W^{\beta}\] \(\alpha \sim N(3.69, 0.502)\) \(\beta \sim N(-0.305, 0.029)\). Growth-based (2022): \[\ln M = 0.28 - 1.30 \ln(L/L_\infty) + 1.08 \ln(k)\] growth-based formulation calibrated using von Bertalanffy parameters, use VB-equivalent \(k\) underlying growth model Gompertz Logistic. use Lorenzen. General applications; meta-analytic contexts; want built-parameter uncertainty original calibration.

title: Natural Mortality Estimation with get_stochastic_mortality()
text: Chen-Watanabe derived von Bertalanffy assumptions, \(k\) parameter specifically means VB growth coefficient. VB model often performs poorly elasmobranch data, especially adult observations sparse. Gompertz Logistic models frequently provide better fits. Historically, researchers faced uncomfortable choice: use best-fitting growth model biological inference abandon CW mortality estimation, force VB fit despite knowing describes data poorly.

title: Natural Mortality Estimation with get_stochastic_mortality()
text: three growth models estimate biological quantities: \(L_\infty\) — asymptotic length \(L_0\) — length birth \(L_{mat}\) — length maturity \(t_{mat}\) — age maturity milestones, can compute von Bertalanffy \(k\) need : \[k_{VB}^{equiv} = \frac{1}{t_{mat}} \ln\left(\frac{L_\infty - L_0}{L_\infty - L_{mat}}\right)\] VB-equivalent \(k\) captures “growth rate information” form Chen-Watanabe can use, regardless growth model generated biological parameters.

title: Partial Pooling for Imbalanced Sex Ratios
text: Consider estimating parameter \(\theta\) (e.g., \(L_{50}\)) sex:

title: Partial Pooling for Imbalanced Sex Ratios
text: Assume sexes share identical parameters: \[\theta_{\text{female}} = \theta_{\text{male}} = \theta\] Problem: Ignores real biological differences sexes.

title: Partial Pooling for Imbalanced Sex Ratios
text: Estimate sex independently: \[\theta_{\text{female}} \perp \theta_{\text{male}}\] Problem: Ignores sexes species. sparse sex gets unreliable estimates.

title: Partial Pooling for Imbalanced Sex Ratios
text: Model sex-specific parameters draws common distribution: \[\theta_s \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \tau^2)\] \(\mu\) species-level mean \(\tau\) controls -sex variation. Key insight: model learns \(\tau\) data: sexes similar → small \(\tau\) → estimates shrink together sexes different → large \(\tau\) → estimates stay separated Sparse sex → borrows strength data-rich sex

title: Partial Pooling for Imbalanced Sex Ratios
text: numerical stability, vitalBayes uses non-centered parameterization: \[\log(\theta_s) = \mu + \tau \cdot \eta_s, \quad \eta_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\] separates global mean (\(\mu\)) sex-specific deviations (\(\eta_s\)), dramatically improves MCMC sampling \(\tau\) small.

title: Partial Pooling for Imbalanced Sex Ratios
text: -sex standard deviation uses half-normal prior: \[\tau \sim \text{Half-Normal}(0, \sigma_\tau)\] \(\sigma_\tau\) set via prior_tau argument. prior: Allows \(\tau = 0\) (complete pooling) data support Permits large \(\tau\) sexes genuinely differ Avoids heavy tails half-Cauchy can cause divergences

title: Cohort Survival Simulation with simulate_survivorship()
text: relationship instantaneous mortality rate \(M(t)\) cumulative survival \(S(t)\) fundamental demographic analysis. cohort exposed age-specific mortality, cumulative survival age \(t\) : \[S(t) = \exp\left(-\int_0^t M() \, da\right)\] function implements relationship via trapezoidal numerical integration mortality schedule. simulation iteration, integral computed yield cumulative survival curve, discrete cohort transitions simulated using binomial survival.

title: Cohort Survival Simulation with simulate_survivorship()
text: cumulative survival curve deterministic given mortality schedule, actual populations experience demographic stochasticity—random variation survives year. function simulates treating age transition binomial process: \[N_{t+1} \sim \text{Binomial}\left(N_t, \frac{S(t+1)}{S(t)}\right)\] \(N_t\) number individuals alive age \(t\), \(S(t+1)/S(t)\) conditional probability surviving age \(t\) age \(t+1\). stochastic formulation means even identical mortality schedules, different simulation runs produce slightly different survival trajectories. variation appropriate projecting small populations demographic stochasticity matters, averaging many iterations recovers expected (deterministic) survival curve.

title: Cohort Survival Simulation with simulate_survivorship()
text: Several biologically meaningful metrics emerge survival simulations: Mean age death computed weighting ages number deaths age: \[\bar{t}_{death} = \frac{\sum_t t \cdot d_t}{\sum_t d_t}\] \(d_t\) number individuals dying age \(t\). Survival maturity proportion birth cohort surviving age \(t_{mat}\), interpolated survival curve: \[S(t_{mat}) = \text{interpolate}(t_{mat}, \{t_i, S_i\})\] Survival maximum age analogously computed \(t_{max}\), representing probability individual birth cohort reaches estimated maximum lifespan.

what: From Birth to Mortality:Bayesian Vital Rates for Elasmobranchs
title: vitalBayes
text: vitalBayes provides coherent Bayesian framework estimating population vital rates elasmobranchs — birth maturity growth natural mortality survival. package implements hierarchical models via Stan precompiled models fast, reliable inference. package addresses critical methodological challenges elasmobranch research: sparse datasets, imbalanced sex ratios, strong parameter correlations, need biologically coherent estimates propagate uncertainty across life stages.

title: vitalBayes

what: 3. Partial Pooling for Imbalanced Sex Ratios
title: vitalBayes
text: problem: Elasmobranch sampling frequently yields imbalanced sex ratios. dataset might contain 150 females 34 males. Fitting separate models produces wide, unreliable credible intervals sparse sex, estimates driven influential observations, inefficient use information (sexes species). Complete pooling (ignoring sex) biologically unrealistic. pooling (fully separate) wastes information. solution: Partial pooling models sex-specific parameters draws common distribution: \[\log(\theta_s) = \mu + \tau \cdot \eta_s, \quad \eta_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)\] μ population mean, τ -sex standard deviation, ηs standardized sex deviations. model learns τ data: sexes appear similar, estimates shrink together; sexes appear different, estimates stay separated; sparse sex borrows strength data-rich sex. Non-centered parameterization: use non-centered form (estimating η rather θ directly) dramatically improves MCMC sampling τ small. Half-normal prior τ: place τ ~ Half-Normal(0, στ) rather commonly-used half-Cauchy. half-Cauchy’s heavy tails can pull τ toward implausibly large values, especially two groups. See vignette("partial_pooling") comprehensive treatment.
code: # Enable partial pooling (especially useful for imbalanced data) data(imbalanced_data)  # 150 females, 34 males  fit <- fit_bayesian_maturity(   maturity    = "mat",   lt          = "fl",    sex         = "sex",   data        = imbalanced_data[embryo == FALSE],   use_pooling = TRUE,    # Hierarchical structure   prior_tau   = 0.5      # Half-normal scale (on log scale) )  # Sex-specific estimates with appropriate shrinkage fit$summary("L50")  # Between-sex difference (still estimable!) fit$summary("L50_diff")

title: vitalBayes
text: problem: Chen-Watanabe mortality model derived von Bertalanffy growth assumptions, requiring specifically VB growth coefficient \(k\). VB model often performs poorly elasmobranch data — adult observations sparse, tends produce biologically implausible \(L_\infty\) estimates (sometimes observed maximum lengths). Gompertz Logistic models frequently fit better, traditionally couldn’t used Chen-Watanabe. solution: vitalBayes computes VB-equivalent \(k\) biological milestones growth models estimate: \[k_{VB}^{equiv} = \frac{1}{t_{mat}} \ln\left(\frac{L_\infty - L_0}{L_\infty - L_{mat}}\right)\] growth coefficient produce von Bertalanffy curve passing biological milestones — regardless growth model generated . Users can fit whichever model best describes data still use Chen-Watanabe mortality estimation. See vignette("chen_watanabe_reparameterization") full mathematical derivation.
code: # Fit Gompertz (assume it fits your data better than VB) gomp_fit <- fit_bayesian_growth(   lt      = "fl",   age     = "age",   sex     = "sex",   data    = growth_data[embryo == FALSE & !is.na(age)],   model   = "gompertz",    # Not VB!   k_based = FALSE,         # Maturity-based parameterization required   birth_fit = birth_fit,   L50_fit   = L50_fit,   t50_fit   = t50_fit )  # Chen-Watanabe mortality from Gompertz fit — this works automatically mort <- get_stochastic_mortality(   method     = "CW",   growth_fit = gomp_fit,   # Any growth model   sex        = 1,   iter       = 2000 )  # The function extracts (Linf, L0, Lmat, tmat) from Gompertz posterior # and computes VB-equivalent k internally

title: vitalBayes
text: problem: traditional Chen-Watanabe formulation uses \(t_0\) (theoretical age length zero) — mathematical artifact biological interpretation can take implausible values growth data sparse. solution: vitalBayes implements L₀-parameterized Chen-Watanabe eliminates \(t_0\) entirely: \[M(t) = \frac{k \cdot L_\infty}{L(t)}\] \(L(t)\) predicted length age. reveals biological mechanism: mortality inversely proportional body size. ratio \(L_\infty / L(t)\) represents far organism maximum size — smaller individuals experience higher mortality. reformulation uses observable quantities (\(L_0\), birth length) rather mathematical abstractions, aligning vitalBayes’s philosophy parameterizing biology, mathematics.

title: vitalBayes
text: problem: Mortality models require growth parameters inputs. Traditional approaches specify independent point estimates uncertainty — e.g., \(L_\infty \sim N(100, 5)\) \(k \sim N(0.1, 0.02)\) — ignoring parameters typically strongly correlated posterior. Independent sampling occasionally generates biologically implausible combinations (high \(L_\infty\) high \(k\)) never appeared original growth model posterior, artificially inflating mortality uncertainty. solution: get_stochastic_mortality() accepts vitalBayes growth fits directly, drawing joint posterior distribution. Parameter correlations preserved, yielding mortality schedules narrower honest uncertainty intervals.
code: # Traditional approach (ignores correlations) mort_naive <- get_stochastic_mortality(   method = "CW",   Linf   = c(100, 5),   # Specified as mean, sd   L0     = c(25, 2),   k      = c(0.1, 0.02),   tmat   = c(10, 1) )  # vitalBayes approach (preserves correlations) mort_joint <- get_stochastic_mortality(   method     = "CW",   growth_fit = growth_fit,  # Full posterior   sex        = 2 )

title: vitalBayes
text: vitalBayes implements three natural mortality models, distinct assumptions: models work growth model fit (VB, Gompertz, Logistic) VB-equivalent \(k\) derivation.
code: # Chen-Watanabe with Gompertz senescence (from any growth model) mort_cw <- get_stochastic_mortality(   method     = "CW",   growth_fit = gomp_fit,   # Works with Gompertz, VB, or Logistic   sex        = 1,   two_phase  = TRUE,   late_model = "gompertz" )  # Peterson-Wroblewski (requires length-weight function) lw_fun <- function(L) 0.0001 * L^3.1 mort_pw <- get_stochastic_mortality(   method     = "PW",   growth_fit = gomp_fit,   sex        = 1,   lw_fun     = lw_fun )  # Lorenzen growth-based (no L-W function needed) mort_lor <- get_stochastic_mortality(   method       = "L",   growth_fit   = gomp_fit,   sex          = 1,   weight_based = FALSE )

text: problem: Specifying priors log-transformed parameters unintuitive. σ = 0.5 log(\(L_{50}\)) mean practical terms? solution: vitalBayes uses coefficient variation (CV) prior specification.
